page_title: Creating a WebSocket server using only the RFC doc (Part 1) : Handshakes 🤝

sources.entry: JavaScript: _Creating a WebSocket server using only the RFC doc (Part 1): Handshakes_

summary.title: Creating a WebSocket server using only the RFC doc (Part 1): Handshakes
summary.one_liner: You learn how the WebSocket opening handshake works per RFC 6455 and how to implement it in a minimal JavaScript (Node.js) server.
takeaways: A WebSocket connection starts as an HTTP GET request with Upgrade headers; the client sends the opening handshake.
The server validates the request (GET, HTTP 1.1+, Host, Upgrade, Connection, Sec-WebSocket-Key of 16 bytes, Sec-WebSocket-Version 13) and rejects invalid ones with 400.
Sec-WebSocket-Accept is computed as base64(SHA-1(key + GUID)) using the RFC's fixed GUID.
On success the server replies with HTTP/1.1 101 Switching Protocols; the server can then use the raw socket to handle the upgrade.
summary.summary: The article builds the opening handshake of a minimal WebSocket server in JavaScript, using RFC 6455 as the only reference. It explains that WebSockets run over HTTP as a GET request with upgrade headers, then walks through the client requirements and the server-side checks. The author uses Node's http server 'upgrade' event, a validation function for the required headers, and a SHA-1 and base64 routine to build Sec-WebSocket-Accept. The article is Part 1 of a series and does not cover sending or receiving messages; the author tests the result with Postman.
